title: Thirty days, then a year
hook: mourning eases after thirty days; Kaddish continues for a parent

segments.voice: Yesterday, shiva: seven days at home, the mourner speaking first. Your line was sit with them. Did you send the meal, or make the visit? Today, what happens when the seven days are over. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-four.

The last chapter of the Torah. Moses climbs a mountain, looks out over the land he will never enter, and dies there. Down below, the people grieve. And the text gives their grief a length. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, the children of Israel "wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days". Then the verse says the days of weeping were ended. The very next line turns to Joshua, and the people listen to him. They don't forget Moses. They can't. But after thirty days, they get up and walk forward. Today's word is that month.
screen: `MOSES DIES ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `THIRTY DAYS OF WEEPING.` → `THEN THEY WALK ON.`

segments.voice: Shloshim. The Hebrew word for thirty. Turn it four ways. First, the text. Moses is mourned for thirty days, and so, the book of Numbers says, is his brother Aaron. Jewish law reads those thirty days as a pattern for every mourner. Second, the steps. Shiva comes first, the low chair and the open door. When it ends, in some communities, the mourners get up and walk together around the block, stepping back into the street for the first time. Then come the rest of the thirty days. Mourners return to work and ordinary errands, but they hold back from parties and celebrations, and some don't cut their hair. Life starts again, but quietly. Third, a parent. For other close relatives, the formal mourning ends at thirty days. For a father or a mother, tradition keeps it going longer, through much of the year, and the child keeps saying the mourner's Kaddish with a congregation, day after day. A parent, the tradition seems to say, takes longer to set down. Fourth, the shape of it. Grief here isn't a switch that turns off on a date. It's a set of doors, each a little wider than the last: the grave, the week, the month, the year. You are walked back into the world one room at a time. Nobody expects you to come out of the first door already healed. They only expect you to keep coming, slowly, and they keep a place for you while you do.
screen: `THIRTY DAYS FOR MOSES.` · `UP FROM THE LOW CHAIR.` · `LONGER FOR A PARENT.` · `DOORS, NOT A SWITCH.` · then, large: `SLOWLY BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: mark one month. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something that changed in your life about a month ago, or something that's still raw. A loss, a move, an ending, a hard conversation. Ask, gently: where am I on the steps? Still on the low chair? Out walking around the block? Back at work but not at the party yet? There's no wrong answer. Then think of one small way to mark the month: a walk, a candle, a line in a notebook. If you pray, you can bring it into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Shloshim. Thirty: the month after a death, when mourners return to life slowly, and for a parent the mourning goes on. Today's word.
Your line: slowly back. Today, mark the month you named, in the small way you chose, and don't rush the next step. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: After shiva, Jewish mourners keep shloshim, the thirty days from the burial: they return to work but avoid celebrations; for a parent the mourning continues through much of the year, with the mourner's Kaddish said in synagogue.
